proposals.evidence: DEDR5079 explicitly records Pengo malkā- lighten alongside Parji melk-/malk- and Gadaba mel-. Zoller pp.689–690 quotes the same Pengo verb from Chandrasekaran; retain its boundary hyphen. The article supports this family independently of the disputed Indo-Aryan comparisons in the surrounding discussion. This family identification does not endorse broader cross-family ancestry claims in the source.

records.Etymology: 1244. Bng. mɔ̄ḷṇɔ, mɔḷmɔḷaṇɔ, ‘to glitter’ and miḷmiḷaṇɔ v.i. ‘to flicker (as light); to flash (lightning)’, kɔḷmɔḷi adj. and kɔḷmɔḷī n.f. ‘burning (as a sensation); shining, sparkling; shine, lustre, sparkle’ and here perhaps umbḷɛ̄ṇɔ v.i. ‘to flicker, waver (e.g., a fire, swarm of flies)’ (with -ɛ-, ɛ̄- suffix). The reduplicated form is found, e.g., in the PAN, describing the ‘flickering’ (i.e. light emitting) crown of King Duryodhana, e.g.: raza Duriodən kɔ barthɛ kɔ mukuṭ mɔḷmɔḷa King Duryodhana GEN.POP stately.OBL GEN.POP crown flickers ‘The stately crown of King Duryodhana flickers’[318] Cf. OIA (AV) kalmali- ‘splendour, brightness, sparkling’ and OIA malmalābhávant- ‘flashing, glittering’. For kalmali- Chandrasekaran (p. 41) suggests Dravidian origin, e.g. found in Tam. mallal ‘elegance, brilliance’, which cannot be the source for the Bng. word, but for which Bomhard suggests PN origin (< *mal-a ‘fullness’ [CINCL 847]). Mayrhofer says about malmalābhávant- (EWA II: 333) with reference to Karl Hoff- mann that the word is ‘sound symbolic rendering of a (visual?) impression (‘Gesichts- eindruck’) through repetitive onomatopoeia’, but Chandrasekaran (p. 42) suggests also for this word Dravidian origin and he quotes as parallels Parji melk- ‘to lighten’, malk- ‘(light) to flash’ and Pengo malkā- ‘to lighten’ (p. 41) which, however, have parallels in Indo-Aryan Ḍog. milk ‘lightning’, Dari. milkala ‘lightning’, N. milkinu ‘(of the sky) to flash with lightning’ and most variants of Ind. ˈmili ‘lightning’ (Hallberg [1992: 211]; Leitner [1889: appendix iv, 14]), Gau. milyõ ‘lightning’, K. vuzmal and Sir.ḍoḍ. uz- muliˈya ‘lightning’ (both are synonym compounds with first component (v)uz- < OIA vidyút- ‘flashing, lightning’ [11742]), and Tibeto-Burman Khm. milak ‘flash, flash of lightning’ and Western Tibetan Balt. melmel ci ‘a very small indistinct glow (of light)’. There is also the H. ideophone milmilānā ‘shine, shimmer, glitter’ (Kellersmann [2017: 609]). Thus, derivation < PIE *(s)mel- ‘give off light smoke, smoulder’ and possible contamination by ‘sound symbolic’ word forms is rather unlikely. Still, if the OIA form can be characterized as ‘repetitive onomatopoeia’ one wonders that it survived unchanged over millennia in a comparatively small area. Note also that the Bng. poet. word barthɔ ‘stately’ is hardly < OIA bhártr̥- ‘husband’ etc. (9402), displaying a rightward displacement of aspiration but rather cognate with bharatá-. However, cf. Pischel § 207 who mentions OIA suffix -tha instead of -ta in M., AMg., JM. Bhāraha. Note also Martirosyan’s perhaps related reconstruction (2013: 112) PIE *mar- mar- reflected in dialectal Arm. *mar-m(a)r-il ‘to shimmer, flicker, glimmer, ex- tinguish gradually (said of e.g. a candle)’ and Greek μαρμαίρω ‘to flash, sparkle, gleam’ (said of any darting, quivering light).
